tip_title: Term Life vs. Whole Life: The Difference Most People Haven't Actually Thought Through
topic: term life vs whole life insurance
blurb:
💡 **Insurance Tip: Term Life vs. Whole Life: The Difference Most People Haven't Actually Thought Through**

Term life insurance covers you for a set period — say 20 or 30 years — and if you die during that window, your beneficiaries get the death benefit. Whole life lasts your entire lifetime and builds a cash value over time, but the premiums run significantly higher for the same coverage amount. Neither one is universally better. Term tends to make more sense when you need a lot of coverage during your working and child-raising years without a huge monthly cost. Whole life tends to come up in conversations about estate planning or when someone wants a permanent policy that doesn't expire.

Not sure which one fits where you are right now? Your Peachy agent can walk through the tradeoffs with you — no pressure, just clarity.

📖 [Learn more from NerdWallet](https://www.nerdwallet.com/insurance/life/learn/term-vs-whole-life-insurance)
summary: Explains the functional difference between term life and whole life insurance — temporary coverage vs. permanent coverage with cash value — framed as a decision framework for readers evaluating which type fits their current life stage.
scoring_notes: Life insurance is evergreen but hasn't been covered in this exact framing — prior life tips focused on coverage amount adequacy and beneficiary review. Term vs. whole is a distinct decision-framework angle. Hits both audiences well: East Cobb's established families and empty nesters are actively holding or reconsidering existing policies; Perimeter's younger professionals are often in the market for the first time. Not seasonal but scores well on relevance across both demographics given the income and family profiles. No prior tip has touched this comparison.

tip_title: Roadside Assistance: You Might Already Have It and Not Know It
blurb:
💡 **Insurance Tip: Roadside Assistance: You Might Already Have It and Not Know It**

A lot of drivers pay for a standalone roadside assistance membership without realizing their auto insurance policy, credit card, or even a manufacturer warranty already includes it. Before you renew or sign up for something new, it's worth checking all three places. The coverage varies — some auto policies include towing, battery jumps, flat tire service, and lockout help as an add-on, while some credit cards offer per-incident roadside service with a flat fee each time you use it. Knowing what you already have (and where the gaps are) keeps you from paying twice for the same protection.

Not sure if roadside is already on your auto policy? Ask your Peachy agent — it takes about two minutes to check.

📖 [Learn more from Consumer Reports](https://www.consumerreports.org/cars/cars-driving/how-to-choose-a-roadside-assistance-plan-a6798450601/)
summary: Covers how roadside assistance coverage may already exist through an auto insurance add-on, credit card benefit, or vehicle warranty — framed as a check-before-you-buy angle to avoid duplicate coverage rather than a comparison of standalone plans.
scoring_notes: Late July is peak road trip and summer driving season — high timeliness. Actionability is strong because the reader can literally check their declarations page or call their card issuer today. Relevant to both audiences: East Cobb's established families with teen drivers and college-age kids; Perimeter's younger professionals who may have coverage they've never verified. No prior tip has touched roadside assistance. Forbes candidate dropped because it named a specific carrier (Allstate) violating the no-carrier-name guardrail; Consumer Reports version is source-appropriate and carrier-neutral.
